title: Nanowave latency concordance — scratch notes
content:
Notes to self: running a focused series of microburst / inter-burst-idle tests — calling this the 'nanowave' pattern (short bursts separated by variable idle). Goal = understand p99+ behavior with small batch timeouts and aggressive KV cache priming.

Date: 2025-09-12 -> 2025-10-03 (iterations)
Setup:
- Model: test-model-v1 (13B, quantized int8 path) served on 1x A10G equivalent
- Runtime: local devpool (dev-2), kernel: tuned-fast-attn, continuous-batcher enabled
- Input length: 32 tokens avg; total seq cap 512
- Traffic shape: nanowave = 8 requests @ 80ms window, then idle 800ms (variable) -> repeat; also tried Poisson lambda 12/s for baseline
- Observability: per-request trace id, token-level latency, kv-hit boolean, batch_size, batch_timeout_ms

Parameters trialed:
- batch_timeout_ms: [2, 4, 8, 16]
- max_batch: 32
- prefill_parallelism: [1,2]
- kv_cache_priming: cold/warm(preload 4 contexts)
- concurrency cap per worker: 6

Representative run (nanowave, warm cache, prefill_parallelism=2):
batch_timeout_ms | p50  | p95  | p99  | p999 | qps (steady inside burst) | avg batch size
-----------------|------|------|------|------|--------------------------|--------------
2 ms             | 18ms | 42ms | 90ms | 180ms| 58.4 qps                 | 1.9          
4 ms             | 20ms | 36ms | 72ms | 140ms| 62.1 qps                 | 2.6          
8 ms             | 24ms | 50ms | 110ms| 230ms| 66.8 qps                 | 4.1          
16 ms            | 33ms | 85ms | 210ms| 520ms| 72.3 qps                 | 7.8          

Observations (quick):
- Lowering batch_timeout to 2–4ms reduces high-percentile tail during short nanowaves, but batch sizes drop -> more work per-token (cpu+gpu overhead), slightly lower median.
- At 16ms timeout we see large p999 spikes tied to long tail when a large batch coincides with cold KV cache (misses).
- Prefill_parallelism=2 consistently reduced p99 by ~10–15% compared to 1, likely overlapping prefill with decode. Good for short bursts.
- Warm KV priming cuts p99 and p999 spikes dramatically for repeated-context patterns (expected). When bursts are random context, priming helps only if cache hit rate > 0.6

Quick ASCII timeline for one run (qps per 100ms window inside 10-burst sample):
[▇▇▇▇▇▇▇▇  ▉▉▉    ▇▇▇▇▇▇   ▉▉] -> shows clear microburst peaks, idle gaps

Weird anomalies / notes:
- 2025-09-20 run had a persistent p999 ~800ms; root cause: kernel selection fallback to scalar path (logging showed kernel oom and fallback). Need to capture kernel metrics during future runs.
- Background noise: small number of stray requests from perf harness (wasn't fully isolated) inflated p999. Rerun with isolated harness scheduled.

Conclusions so far (rough):
- For nanowave pattern, sweet spot seems batch_timeout 4ms + prefill_parallelism=2 + KV warmup when contexts repeat -> good p95/p99 balance and decent qps.
- Don't push timeout >8ms if you care about p999 for short bursts. If workload is continuous high qps, larger timeout helps throughput and unit cost.

Next steps / TODO (short):
- Add kernel-level telemetry correlation (INFR-4213) -> pair with PR #1789
- Re-run isolated harness with strict ingress shaping (no stray traffic) and collect 3 seeds per setting
- Test hetero fleet: A10G vs A100 p99 delta for same configs (cheap vs fast)
- Try fractional batching: accept partial batch discount heuristics (see notes in slack thread)
- Plot overlay charts (p95/p99/p999 vs batch_timeout) and export for product brief

Unresolved questions / hypotheses:
- Is prefill_parallelism >2 worth it (diminishing returns vs context switching)? Need microbench of GPU overlap.
- Could dynamic timeout per-tenant (short for bursty clients) be automated at routing layer? How to detect nanowave pattern cheaply?

Notes to self: keep this doc minimal. Marking follow-up items in Jira: INFR-4213 linked above. Share with Maya for charting.
